questions.explain: An effusion distends the hip capsule, and flexion, abduction and external rotation maximise capsular volume and minimise pain. Flexion-adduction-internal rotation is the posture of a posterior hip dislocation.
questions.note: Septic hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old has 4 days of fever and focal distal femoral tenderness; CRP 95 mg/L, ESR 70 mm/h, and the femoral X-ray is normal. What is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: No imaging; a normal X-ray excludes osteomyelitis
questions.explain: Plain films remain normal for 10-14 days in osteomyelitis; MRI is most sensitive and shows marrow oedema and subperiosteal abscess. CT is less sensitive early and involves radiation.
questions.note: MRI best for osteomyelitis (high ESR, normal X-ray → MRI).

questions.stem: A 10-month-old has distal femoral metaphyseal osteomyelitis and develops a swollen knee effusion. What anatomical feature explains the joint involvement at this age?
options: Transphyseal vessels connecting metaphysis and epiphysis
An intra-articular metaphysis at the distal femur
Absence of a periosteum in infancy
A cartilaginous growth plate acting as a conduit for pus
questions.explain: Under 18 months, blood vessels cross the physis, so metaphyseal infection spreads into the epiphysis and joint; after the physis becomes a barrier, contiguous joint spread occurs mainly where the metaphysis is intra-articular (hip, shoulder, elbow, ankle).
questions.note: Under 18 months, transphyseal vessels spread infection to the joint.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with uncomplicated MSSA osteomyelitis of the tibia has become afebrile with a falling CRP after 3 days of IV cefazolin. What is the best plan?
options: Continue IV therapy for 6 weeks via a peripherally inserted central line
Stop antibiotics now, as the CRP is falling
Switch to oral therapy for 5 days in total
Switch to oral therapy to complete about 3 weeks in total
questions.explain: Current evidence supports a short IV phase (2-4 days) then oral antibiotics once clinically improving, for about 3 weeks in total for uncomplicated disease. Prolonged IV courses add line complications without benefit.
questions.note: Short IV (2-4 days) → oral; about 3 weeks total.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a hot swollen knee; aspiration yields purulent fluid with Gram-positive cocci in clusters. IV antibiotics have been started. What else is required?
questions.explain: Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency: proteolytic enzymes in pus destroy articular cartilage within hours, so the joint needs urgent washout in addition to antibiotics. Steroids into an infected joint are contraindicated.
questions.note: Septic arthritis: joint washout; drain subperiosteal abscess, remove sequestrum.

cards.front: Which organisms cause osteomyelitis and septic arthritis at different ages and settings?
cards.back: S. aureus most common • Kingella kingae 6 mo-4 y • GBS/E. coli neonates • Salmonella in sickle cell • Pseudomonas after nail puncture.

cards.front: How do you investigate a child with suspected bone or joint infection?
cards.back: Blood culture, CRP, ESR • ultrasound for effusion • X-ray normal for 10-14 days • joint aspiration: Gram stain, culture, PCR • MRI best for osteomyelitis.

cards.front: Outline treatment of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
cards.back: MSSA: nafcillin/oxacillin/dicloxacillin, IV cefazolin; MRSA: clindamycin or vancomycin • short IV (2-4 d) → oral, ~3 weeks total • septic arthritis: joint washout • drain subperiosteal abscess, remove sequestrum.

II-20.summary: Screen hips with Ortolani (relocates) and Barlow (dislocates), image with ultrasound before ~4.5 months and X-ray after, and treat early with a Pavlik harness; clubfoot is Ponseti casting; OI (type I collagen) must be considered before labelling fractures as abuse; achondroplasia is FGFR3 gain-of-function with rhizomelia and foramen magnum stenosis.

questions.stem: During the newborn hip examination, the examiner abducts the flexed hip and lifts the greater trochanter, feeling a 'clunk'. What does a positive result indicate?
options: A located hip that has been dislocated
A benign ligamentous click without instability
A dislocated hip that has been relocated
questions.explain: Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip (abduction + anterior lift); Barlow dislocates a located but unstable hip (adduction + posterior push). A fixed dislocation cannot be relocated and is Ortolani-negative.
questions.note: Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip; Barlow dislocates a located one.

questions.stem: Which newborn has the highest risk of developmental dysplasia of the hip?
options: A second-born boy delivered vaginally at 38 weeks
A preterm boy born at 32 weeks by cephalic delivery
A girl born at term by vaginal delivery to a mother with gestational diabetes
A first-born girl delivered by caesarean section for breech presentation
questions.explain: Breech position, female sex, first-born status and family history are the major risk factors (plus oligohydramnios and tight swaddling). Caesarean section does not remove the risk from breech positioning in utero.
questions.note: DDH: breech, family history, female sex, first-born, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old girl born breech has a normal hip examination. Which imaging is appropriate?
options: No imaging if the examination is normal
questions.explain: The femoral head is cartilaginous and invisible on X-ray in early infancy, so ultrasound is used before about 4.5 months; breech babies get ultrasound even with a normal exam. X-ray becomes useful once the ossific nucleus appears.
questions.note: Hip ultrasound before about 4.5 months; X-ray afterwards.

questions.stem: A 7-week-old has an Ortolani-positive left hip confirmed as dislocated on ultrasound. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Closed reduction and hip spica cast
Double nappies and review at 6 months
questions.explain: Under 6 months a Pavlik harness holds the hips flexed and abducted, allowing the femoral head to mould the acetabulum. Closed then open reduction are reserved for failed harness or late presentation; double nappies are ineffective.
questions.note: DDH: Pavlik harness under 6 months → closed → open reduction.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old girl walks with a limp and has a shorter left leg, asymmetric thigh creases and restricted left hip abduction. Ortolani and Barlow tests are negative. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A normal hip, as Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative
Established developmental dysplasia with fixed dislocation
questions.explain: Ortolani and Barlow tests become negative once the dislocation is fixed and soft tissues contract; limited abduction and leg-length discrepancy are the late signs. Perthes typically presents at 4-8 years.
questions.note: DDH: Barlow/Ortolani positive; later limited abduction, leg-length discrepancy.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old presents with a femoral fracture after a minor fall; X-ray shows osteopenia and old healing rib fractures. The baby has blue sclerae and the father had several fractures as a child. Which diagnosis must be considered before attributing the fractures to abuse?
options: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
questions.explain: OI (defective type I collagen, usually AD COL1A1/COL1A2) causes low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae and a positive family history, and must be considered in suspected non-accidental injury; it does not exclude abuse but changes the evaluation.
questions.note: Consider OI in non-accidental injury. Scoliosis: forward bend test → X-ray.

questions.stem: A newborn has short proximal limbs, macrocephaly with frontal bossing and trident hands; the father is 52 years old and of normal stature. What is the molecular mechanism?
options: Loss-of-function mutation in COL1A1 reducing type I collagen
Mutation in fibrillin-1 weakening connective tissue
Gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 impairing endochondral ossification
Loss-of-function mutation in the SHOX gene on the sex chromosomes
questions.explain: Achondroplasia is caused by a constitutively active FGFR3 that inhibits chondrocyte proliferation in growth plates, giving rhizomelic shortening; most cases are de novo mutations associated with advanced paternal age.
questions.note: FGFR3 overactive → poor endochondral growth → rhizomelic limbs.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl has a positive forward bend test; standing X-ray shows a thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 34° and she has 2 years of growth remaining. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observation with repeat X-ray in 6-12 months
questions.explain: Per the notes, curves of 30-40° in a growing child are braced to prevent progression; 10-30° is monitored and >40-50° needs surgery. (Many guidelines start bracing from ~25° in skeletally immature patients.)
questions.note: Scoliosis Cobb 10-30°: monitor; 30-40°: brace; >40-50°: surgery.

cards.front: How is developmental dysplasia of the hip screened, diagnosed and treated?
cards.back: Risk: breech, female, first-born, family history, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling • Ortolani relocates, Barlow dislocates • later: limited abduction, LLD • US <4.5 mo, X-ray after • Pavlik <6 mo → closed → open reduction.

cards.front: Describe clubfoot and its management.
cards.back: Rigid CAVE deformity: cavus, adductus, varus, equinus • Ponseti serial casting → Achilles tenotomy → bracing.

cards.front: Compare osteogenesis imperfecta and achondroplasia.
cards.back: OI: COL1A1/COL1A2 (usually AD), defective type I collagen → low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae; consider in NAI; IV bisphosphonates • Achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain-of-function, older fathers → rhizomelia, macrocephaly, trident hands, foramen magnum stenosis.
